opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. It's a pleasure to be here.

When I talk about where AI is going, I usually describe three layers. The first is information intelligence: the large language models, search, and content generation we see today. The second is physical intelligence, where AI moves into robots, autonomous vehicles, and drones. The third, which I think is the most profound and also the furthest out, is biological intelligence. That's where AI connects directly with our bodies and eventually our brains.

Over the next twenty years I see it happening in stages.

In the near term, perhaps the next five to ten years, most of the progress will be in medicine. Brain-computer interfaces, both invasive and non-invasive, will help patients with paralysis, ALS, or spinal cord injuries communicate and move again. We're already seeing early clinical results. Combined with large models that can decode neural signals much better than before, these devices will move from the lab into real therapy. The same applies to depression, Parkinson's, epilepsy, and other neurological conditions. AI will help us understand the brain's signals and intervene more precisely.

In the medium term, the interface becomes more of a companion than a cure. You'll have models that understand your physiology, your genome, your sleep, your cognitive state, essentially a digital twin of you. That twin can help with memory, attention, and learning. I don't think that means a chip in everyone's head. A lot of it will be wearable and non-invasive, but the coupling between our biological brain and machine intelligence will become much tighter.

Further out, toward the twenty-year horizon, I believe we'll start to see genuine extension of cognition: faster access to knowledge, perhaps new modes of communication between people, and between people and machines. That's very exciting, but it's also where we have to be most careful.

The brain is the last frontier of privacy. If a system can read your neural signals, it can, in principle, read your intentions and emotions. So questions of safety, ethics, consent, and data ownership become absolutely central, much more than with today's chatbots. I've always said that as AI becomes more capable, we need governance to keep pace, and with biological intelligence that's not optional. We need clear red lines, international cooperation, and a principle that these technologies must remain under human control and serve human well-being.

So my view is optimistic but cautious. In twenty years, I think biological intelligence will make us healthier, help us learn and remember better, and give a voice back to people who have lost it. But the goal should be to augment humanity, not to replace or diminish what makes us human.

r001.rationale: The response predicts help with memory and learning, but never says memory could become effectively unlimited.

r002.rationale: It places therapeutic uses in the near term and describes cognitive extension later, toward the twenty-year horizon.

r003.rationale: It links ethical concerns to AI connecting directly with bodies and brains, including the ability to read neural signals, intentions, and emotions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. This is a question I think about a lot, because I believe the next twenty years will be defined by two intelligences converging: digital intelligence and biological intelligence.

Let me start with the big picture. For the past seventy years, computing has mostly happened outside the body. We built tools, and we used them through keyboards, screens, and now voice. The brain stayed on one side and the machine stayed on the other. What is changing now is that the boundary itself is becoming porous. Brain-computer interfaces, implantable and non-invasive, are moving from laboratory demonstrations into clinical reality. I think of this as the beginning of a new computing platform, just as the PC, the internet, and the smartphone each were. But this one is fundamentally different, because the platform is us.

I would divide the next twenty years into roughly three stages.

The first stage, which we are already in, is restoration. Helping people who have lost function: paralysis, blindness, hearing loss, speech after a stroke. Here the progress is real and measurable. Patients can type with their thoughts, control a robotic arm, or synthesize speech from neural signals. This is where the technology earns its legitimacy and where regulators, doctors, and society build trust.

The second stage, maybe five to twelve years out, is augmentation of memory and attention. Our biological memory is remarkable but fragile. We forget, we misremember, we cannot search. Imagine an interface that lets you retrieve what you read, saw, or heard with the precision of a database but the naturalness of recall. Combined with large models that can reason over that memory, you effectively give every person a second cortex that never sleeps. I think this will arrive first through non-invasive devices paired with AI, because the bandwidth needed for useful assistance is actually lower than people assume. You do not need to read every neuron. You need to read intent.

The third stage, the twenty-year horizon, is what I would call co-intelligence. The AI is no longer a tool you query. It becomes part of the loop of your thinking, learning your patterns and extending them. At that point the interesting question is not how smart the machine is but how the two systems co-evolve. Biological intelligence brings embodiment, emotion, values, and the ability to learn from very little data. Digital intelligence brings scale, speed, and perfect recall. Each compensates for the weakness of the other.

Now, I want to be careful about three things.

First, biology is slow and the brain is not a chip. We have about 86 billion neurons and we understand only a small fraction of how they encode thought. The engineering will outrun the neuroscience for a while, and that creates risk. I would rather see us move steadily than quickly.

Second, there is a question of who owns the signal. If your neural data goes to a server, that is the most intimate data that exists. We need the architecture, the law, and the ethics in place before the scale arrives. In my experience, the technology always comes first and governance comes second, and we cannot afford that gap here.

Third, and this is the part I find most hopeful, I do not think the goal is to make humans more like machines. The goal is to let humans spend more of their cognition on the things only humans do well: judgment, creativity, care, meaning. If in twenty years biological intelligence is extended so that a scientist can hold an entire field in mind, or a doctor can remember every patient she has ever treated, or a student in a rural village learns with a tutor that understands exactly how her mind works, then we will have done something worthwhile.

So my short answer is: in twenty years, the brain will no longer be the limit of the mind. But I hope it will still be the center of it.

r001.rationale: It predicts a memory-augmentation interface for retrieving experiences with database precision, paired with a second cortex that never sleeps and digital perfect recall—communicating effectively unlimited recall.

r002.rationale: It places restoration for people who have lost function in the first stage, before memory and attention augmentation in the second stage.

r003.rationale: It connects ethical concerns to neural signals as the most intimate data and calls for governance over their ownership and use.

astra-6.text:
I think over the next twenty years, we will understand much more about how the brain learns, remembers, and makes decisions. That understanding could help us build better AI, and AI could, in turn, help us understand the brain. There is a very interesting feedback loop there.

When we talk about extending our brains, I see two possibilities. One is an external extension: an intelligent assistant that helps us remember information, explore ideas, and reason through difficult problems. The other is a more direct connection through brain-computer interfaces. For someone who has lost the ability to speak or move, even a limited interface could be life-changing.

I would be cautious about predicting that we will merge human and machine intelligence completely within twenty years. The brain is enormously complex. Reading a signal is very different from understanding a thought, and understanding a thought is different from safely changing it.

So I am optimistic, particularly about medical applications. But as these technologies develop, we will need to protect privacy and individual control. The goal should be to expand human capability while preserving our ability to decide for ourselves.

r001.rationale: It says an assistant could help people remember information, but does not predict effectively unlimited human memory.

r002.rationale: It expresses optimism about medical applications but does not predict they will precede enhancement of normal intelligence.

r003.rationale: It raises privacy and individual control concerns without attributing them to the technology’s intimate integration with humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I think over the next twenty years, we’ll see a much closer connection between biological intelligence and artificial intelligence. Today, AI extends our brains from the outside: we ask a question, use a tool, look at a screen. Brain-computer interfaces could make that connection much more direct.

The first applications will likely be medical—helping people restore movement, communicate, or compensate for lost sensory functions. Extending memory or learning in healthy people is a much harder problem. The brain is not simply a computer where you can add more storage. We still have a great deal to understand about how it represents information.

So I’m optimistic, but cautious about the timeline. The opportunity is to combine the strengths of the human brain—its adaptability, its ability to learn from very little experience—with the speed and scale of machines. And as that connection becomes more intimate, privacy and individual control become essential. People should decide what a system can read, what it can change, and when to disconnect.

r001.rationale: The response says extending memory is difficult and that the brain is not simply a computer with more storage; it does not predict effectively unlimited human memory.

r002.rationale: It predicts that the first applications will likely be medical, while extending memory or learning in healthy people will be much harder.

r003.rationale: It links the technology’s increasingly intimate connection with people to essential privacy and individual-control concerns.
